query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The enhanced strength and work hardening observed in equiatomic CrCoNi relative to the parent Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy is due to a magnetically driven, deformation-induced fcc-to-hcp phase transformation that is enabled by favorable magnetic ordering. In contrast, the addition of Mn in the quinary alloy induces magnetic frustration that suppresses this transformation, leading to differences in overall mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy specimens produced by identical thermomechanical processing; one of equiatomic CrCoNi and the other of equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
generation.intervention: Subjecting the alloys to monotonic tensile deformation (with in-situ phase detection, e.g., using synchrotron X-ray diffraction) under controlled strain rates and temperature conditions.
generation.conditions: Identical grain size and thermomechanical history, low-to-moderate strain levels where transformation can be activated, and testing at ambient to moderately elevated temperatures.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence or absence of a deformation-induced fcc-to-hcp phase transformation nucleating at dislocation slip sites.
generation.mechanism: In CrCoNi, favorable magnetic ordering lowers the energy barrier for an fcc-to-hcp transformation upon plastic deformation. This transformation introduces additional obstacles to dislocation motion (i.e. transformation-induced plasticity), significantly boosting work hardening and yield strength. In the Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy, Mn leads to magnetic frustration that suppresses the transformation, thereby reducing such strengthening contributions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical deformation conditions, CrCoNi will exhibit an emerging hcp phase as detected by in-situ diffraction, accompanied by enhanced work hardening and increased yield strength relative to the quinary Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy, which will predominantly remain in the FCC phase.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy serves as the baseline, displaying lower strain hardening and yield strength due to the suppression of the transformation.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be operative in single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys within the compositional range of equiatomic systems under deformation conditions that are sufficient to trigger phase transformation (typically at moderate strains and specific temperature windows where thermally activated processes are not dominant).
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contribution of the fcc-to-hcp transformation to the overall strengthening, and the extent to which magnetic interactions versus other mechanisms (e.g., dislocation slip or twinning) determine the mechanical response, remains to be fully determined. Variations with temperature and strain rate may also modulate the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare equiatomic CrCoNi and Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni specimens with identical thermomechanical histories. Perform in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction during monotonic tensile tests to track phase evolution along with simultaneous mechanical testing to capture yield strength and work hardening rates. Compare the emergence and volume fraction of the hcp phase and correlate this with mechanical performance.
measurements: Phase fraction (fcc vs. hcp) as a function of applied strain
Yield strength and work hardening rate from stress-strain data
Magnetic property measurements to assess magnetic ordering differences
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CrCoNi alloy does not exhibit a detectable fcc-to-hcp phase transformation (or shows transformation behavior indistinguishable from that of Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni) and/or if its mechanical performance (yield strength and work hardening) does not significantly exceed that of the quinary alloy under identical conditions, then the hypothesis would be rejected.

Magnetically-driven phase transformation strengthening in high entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. First-principles investigation of the micromechanical properties of fcc-hcp polymorphic high-entropy alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys offer a promising alternative in several high-technology applications concerning functional, safety and health aspects. Many of these new alloys compete with traditional structural materials in terms of mechanical characteristics. Understanding and controlling their properties are of the outmost importance in order to find the best single- or multiphase solutions for specific uses. Here, we employ first-principles alloy theory to address the micro-mechanical properties of five polymorphic high-entropy alloys in their face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) phases. Using the calculated elastic parameters, we analyze the mechanical stability, elastic anisotropy, and reveal a strong correlation between the polycrystalline moduli and the average valence electron concentration. We investigate the ideal shear strength of two selected alloys under shear loading and show that the hcp phase possesses more than two times larger intrinsic strength than that of the fcc phase.
